archetype.name: Bubble Team (process ahead of results)
archetype.definition: A Washington club that controls 5-on-5 play well enough to make the playoffs but is giving it back in its own net and on special teams, leaving it fifth in the Metropolitan on a 91-point pace.

report.headline: Good 5-on-5 team, leaky crease: the November slide is a goaltending problem
report.take:
Washington is 10-8-0, fifth in the Metropolitan and 19th of 32 on the site, and the record undersells how it plays at even strength. Its 53.7% expected-goals share ranks 6th in the league and the offense is 9th at 3.44 goals a game. A team with those numbers should be pushing the top three in the division. Instead it allows 3.61 goals a game, 28th, and its goal differential sits at minus 3.

The gap between the chances and the scoreboard is mostly in goal. Team save percentage is .882, 25th, against a league average of .892, and the goaltending group grades a D. Logan Thompson has been roughly average (.888, +0.5 GSAx over 13 starts). Charlie Lindgren has not (.867, -2.6 in five starts). That is new for this franchise. Its goalies were +25.1 GSAx last season and +21.4 the year before, and those years produced a top-eight defense both times. Weak special teams make it worse: the PP at 20% and the PK at 75.4% both rank in the low 20s. Wingers have also been getting loose, with 46.1% of the points Washington allows going to wingers against a league norm of 38.1%.

The offense has its own soft spots. Alex Tuch's 11 goals on 45 shots are carrying a forward group graded only C-. Alex Ovechkin has one goal on 32 shots while playing 13.62 minutes a night. Dylan Strome (16 points) and Ryan Leonard (14) are producing, but the scoring leader is hot rather than steady. The blueline is the deepest group, graded B-. Cole Hutson ranks 13th of 259 defensemen with 15 points, and Jakob Chychrun logs 24.4 minutes. Timothy Liljegren (209th, 48.4% xGF) is a real hole in the third pair.

The direction is the worry. October went 8-4. November is 2-4 with 4.67 goals allowed a game, including back-to-back losses to New Jersey in which Washington gave up 12. The underlying shot share hasn't collapsed, so this reads as a team whose goaltending and penalty kill are failing a decent structure. Some save-percentage recovery is likely given the team's history. Whether it comes soon enough depends on Thompson carrying a heavier load.

strengths.title: Wins the 5-on-5 chance battle
strengths.body: Washington's expected-goals share ranks 6th, well above the league's 50%. That shows a team generating better looks than it allows at even strength. Nearly every regular forward sits above 52% xGF, so it is depth of play rather than one line. Possession is only even, so the edge comes from shot quality more than volume, which tends to be the more durable kind.

strengths.title: Hutson and Chychrun drive the blueline
strengths.body: Cole Hutson ranks 13th among 259 defensemen with 15 points and a 55.5% xGF. Jakob Chychrun plays 24.4 minutes a night with 13 points. Together they run the power play from the back, with five PP points each. That two-man engine is real, but the group's B- grade is propped up by them while Liljegren and Fehervary contribute little offensively.

strengths.title: Offense scoring above league average
strengths.body: At 3.44 goals a game Washington is 9th, comfortably ahead of the league's 3.17. Shooting at 12.2% (9th) helps. So does Tuch's burst, which will likely cool. Leonard and Strome supply a steadier base underneath it, and Ovechkin's one goal on 32 shots suggests some scoring is still owed from his line.

concerns.title: Goaltending has fallen off a cliff
concerns.body: Team save percentage is .882, 25th, and team GSAx has gone from +25.1 last season to -0.9. Lindgren's .867 and -2.6 GSAx in five starts are the sharpest drag. Thompson has been merely average. The franchise's recent history argues for some bounce-back, but a D-graded crease cannot support a 28th-ranked goals-against.

concerns.title: Goals against are getting worse
concerns.body: Washington has allowed 4.6 goals a game over its last five, nearly a full goal above its season rate. November's 2-4 record came with 4.67 allowed a game. With the shot share holding steady, this points to saves and the penalty kill (75.4%, 20th) rather than a structural collapse. It still has to stop before it buries the October cushion.

concerns.title: Opposing wingers are feasting
concerns.body: Washington ranks 28th at holding wingers to their usual production. Wingers take 46.1% of the points it allows, far above the league's 38.1%. That points to coverage breakdowns on the flanks and on the weak side, exactly where a struggling goalie gets exposed. Liljegren's 48.4% xGF, the worst among regular defensemen, fits the pattern.

trend.note: An 8-4 October gave way to a 2-4 November in which the goals against ballooned. The last five games went 2-3 with a minus-5 differential and back-to-back losses to New Jersey.

weekAhead.headline: Two top-five road tests around a get-right game with Buffalo
weekAhead.body:
The week opens in Tampa and closes in Boston, the site's 4th- and 5th-ranked teams. Sandwiched between is a home game against 22nd-ranked Buffalo. Tampa is the stronger 5-on-5 team (56.3% xGF, 3rd) with an A-graded blueline, so Washington's usual chance edge is unlikely to show up there. Boston leans on elite goaltending (.911, 3rd; +10.9 GSAx) and the second-highest all-situations PDO in the league, a profile that should cool eventually but is hard to beat in its own building.

Buffalo is the game Washington has to win. The Sabres' goaltending grades D-, their all-situations PDO is last in the league, and their defense allows the most to centers of any team. Washington already beat them once in overtime in October. A split of the two road games plus a win at home would be a good week given the recent defensive form. Anything less extends the slide.

keyMatchups.title: Washington PP vs Tampa's soft PK
keyMatchups.body: Tampa kills only 71.7% of penalties, 25th in the league. That is the clearest weakness in an otherwise strong team. Washington's 20% power play has been below average, but Hutson and Chychrun running the point gives it a chance to steal goals where 5-on-5 chances will be scarce.

keyMatchups.title: Washington centers vs Buffalo's defense
keyMatchups.body: Buffalo ranks last at holding centers to their usual output, and its goalies sit near the bottom in save percentage. Strome (16 points) and a productive Dubois should find room. This is the game where Washington's offense should run hot.

keyMatchups.title: Beating Boston's hot goaltending
keyMatchups.body: Boston's .911 save percentage and 104.1 PDO lead much of the league. Its 4th-ranked defense is built more on saves than on suppression, since it allows more shots than average. Washington will need volume and traffic, and Ovechkin's line is due to convert.

weekAhead.watch: Who starts in goal and whether the save percentage climbs back toward league average. Thompson carrying the two road games would signal the staff has seen enough of Lindgren's numbers.

restOfSeason.body:
The 5-on-5 game says this is a playoff-caliber team. The goaltending says it is a bubble team. Washington's goalies have been well above average for two straight seasons, so a team save percentage stuck in the bottom eight seems unlikely to last, and if it recovers the goals against should drift down from the current extreme. Some scoring regression is also coming, from Tuch in particular, but Ovechkin's drought and a solid shot rate should offset part of it. Expect the goal differential to move back toward even and the record to settle around its current 91-point pace, with upside if Thompson holds the net.

The ceiling is limited by the C- forward group, below-average special teams on both sides, and a strong Metropolitan top three. The realistic target is a wild-card fight. I project roughly 89-97 points and 41-46 wins, with goals allowed per game falling to about 3.0-3.3 if the goaltending normalizes.
swingFactors: Thompson's save percentage over a heavier workload
Penalty kill climbing back toward league average
Ovechkin and the depth forwards replacing Tuch's cooling finish

confidence.note: 18 games is a small sample, but the 5-on-5 numbers and the goaltending history point in a consistent direction.
